claims.text: Progressive resistance training creates mechanical tension, the main non-drug training stimulus for increasing muscle mass.

cite.quote: mechanical tension through progressive overload with RET is the most potent non-pharmacological stimulus and external variable for increasing skeletal muscle mass

claims.text: Progressive overload means gradually and systematically increasing training stress over time.

cite.locator: Resistance Training Variables Explained, Core Principles of Resistance Training
cite.quote: This involves a gradual and systematic increase in training stress over time.

claims.text: About 6–12 reps, 3–6 sets and 60–80% of one-rep max is a practical moderate-load template.

cite.locator: Section 4, Training Principles for Muscle Hypertrophy
cite.quote: Implementation of training with moderate number of repetitions (~6−12), multiple sets (3−6), moderate loads (60−80% 1RM), and short rest intervals (60 s)

claims.text: There is no single required hypertrophy rep zone: similar whole-muscle growth can occur across loads of roughly 30% 1RM and above.

cite.locator: Section 3, Hypertrophy, Conclusions and Practical Applications
cite.quote: similar whole muscle growth (i.e., muscle thickness, CSA) can be achieved across a wide spectrum of loading ranges ≥ ~30% 1RM

claims.text: A Cambridge mathematical model estimated 70% of maximum load as more efficient than lighter loading; this is model-based, not a universal prescription.

cite.quote: our model suggests that loads of 70% are a more efficient method of stimulating growth

claims.text: Resistance can come from free weights, body weight, bands or machines.

cite.locator: Truth #2: You Need to Challenge Your Muscles
cite.quote: The resistance can come from lifting weights, using your body as a weight, pulling resistance bands, or pushing and pulling machines like gym equipment.

claims.text: Compound exercises move multiple joints and train several muscle groups at once.

cite.locator: Exercise and Equipment Selection, Compound vs. Isolation Exercises
cite.quote: Compound exercises are multi-joint movements that engage multiple muscle groups simultaneously, such as the squat, deadlift, bench press, overhead press, and row.

claims.text: Isolation exercises are single-joint movements used to target a particular muscle group more directly.

cite.locator: Exercise and Equipment Selection, Compound vs. Isolation Exercises
cite.quote: Isolation exercises are single-joint movements that target a specific muscle group, such as the bicep curl, triceps extension, leg extension, or calf raise.

claims.text: A general starting point is to train every major muscle group two or three times per week.

cite.locator: Truth #2: You Need to Challenge Your Muscles
cite.quote: Aim to work all major muscle groups — chest, back, arms, legs, shoulders, and core — 2 to 3 times each week.

claims.text: Allow roughly 48–72 hours before challenging the same muscle group again.

cite.locator: Truth #3: Muscles Grow When You Rest
cite.quote: recommend that you take 48 to 72 hours between resistance training workouts that challenge the same muscle group.

claims.text: Muscle gain requires enough energy; eating a little more than usual can support growth.

cite.locator: Truth #4: Muscles Need the Right Fuel
cite.quote: You must eat enough calories; a little more than when you are not working on building muscles.

claims.text: Pair resistance training with adequate dietary protein to support muscle protein synthesis.

cite.quote: protein intake alongside RT is a potent stimulus for muscle protein synthesis.

claims.text: Most people should aim for 7–9 hours of quality sleep to support muscle-building recovery.

cite.locator: Truth #3: Muscles Grow When You Rest
cite.quote: Most people need 7–9 h of quality sleep to support their muscle-building goals.
